meta.subject: Chemistry
meta.summary: A solution is a uniform mixture, and this unit is about two things: how much solute is in it (concentration, Henry's law, Raoult's law) and what the dissolved particles do to the solvent (the four **colligative properties**). The numericals are predictable and score well: almost every board paper since 2019 has asked a colligative-property calculation with the van't Hoff factor, plus a theory question on deviations from Raoult's law or azeotropes.
pattern: Unit weightage in 2026-27: **7 marks** out of 70 (CBSE curriculum 2026-27). The paper has 33 questions; calculators and log tables are **not allowed**, so numbers are chosen to divide neatly.

**1-mark items (Section A)**: almost every set has one or two - which solution has the lowest freezing point / highest osmotic pressure, azeotrope type from boiling point, Henry's constant and temperature, and assertion-reason on ideal solutions or colligative properties.

**2-mark items (Section B)**: deviation from Raoult's law with reason (phenol + aniline, ethanol + acetone, chloroform + acetone appeared in 2026 sets), Henry's law applications (bends, anoxia), azeotrope definitions, two-step numericals.

**3-mark numericals (Section C)**: the favourites are association of benzoic / acetic acid in benzene (2020, 2023, 2025, 2026), freezing point or boiling point of an electrolyte solution with complete dissociation (MgSO$_4$, MgBr$_2$, CaCl$_2$, Na$_2$SO$_4$), molar mass from lowering of vapour pressure (the '31.84 mm Hg' family: 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026), and ethylene glycol antifreeze.

**4-mark case studies (Section D)** on this unit appeared in 2023 (compartment), 2024 (compartment), 2025 (main) and 2026 (main): passages on osmosis, Raoult's law and azeotropes with one calculation inside.
**5-mark questions (Section E)** in 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 combined a numerical (3 marks) with two short theory parts (Henry's law, ideal solution definition, van't Hoff factor below 1).

inSyllabus: Expressing concentration of solutions (mass %, volume %, mass by volume %, ppm, mole fraction, molarity, molality)
Solubility - of solids and of gases in liquids (Henry's law)
Vapour pressure of liquid solutions (Raoult's law)
Colligative properties and determination of molar mass
Abnormal molar masses and the van't Hoff factor
syllabus.note: Nothing inside this unit is excluded in 2026-27. Separately, CBSE moved four other Class XII topics to formative (school) assessment only - Surface Chemistry, General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements, Polymers and Chemistry in Everyday Life - so older papers' questions on colloids or polymers are not in the board exam.

Small rounding differences (e.g. 97.5% vs the scheme's 97.6%) are noted on the questions.

Two official answers needed comment: NCERT's printed answer to Exercise 1.26 (5 M) assumes the solution weighs 1 kg; and the 2025-26 SQP marking scheme prints 22.9 mm Hg for Q22 where its own expression gives 22.8 mm Hg. Both are explained where they appear.

keyPoints: Molarity changes with temperature (volume changes); mass %, ppm, mole fraction and molality do not.
Henry's law: $p = K_H x$. Higher $K_H$ means lower solubility. $K_H$ rises with temperature, so gases dissolve less in warm water.
Raoult's law (volatile components): $p_i = x_i p_i^\circ$; $p_{	ext{total}} = p_1^\circ + (p_2^\circ - p_1^\circ)x_2$. The vapour is richer in the more volatile component.
Raoult's law is a special case of Henry's law with $K_H = p_1^\circ$.
Ideal solution: obeys Raoult's law at all concentrations, $\Delta_{mix}H = 0$, $\Delta_{mix}V = 0$, A-B forces equal A-A and B-B forces (benzene + toluene, n-hexane + n-heptane).

Positive deviation: A-B weaker, vapour pressure higher, $\Delta_{mix}H > 0$, $\Delta_{mix}V > 0$ (ethanol + acetone, CS$_2$ + acetone) - forms minimum boiling azeotropes (ethanol-water, about 95% ethanol by volume).

Negative deviation: A-B stronger, vapour pressure lower, $\Delta_{mix}H < 0$, $\Delta_{mix}V < 0$ (phenol + aniline, chloroform + acetone) - forms maximum boiling azeotropes (HNO$_3$ 68% + water 32% by mass, 393.5 K).
Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles, not their nature: relative lowering of vapour pressure, $\Delta T_b$, $\Delta T_f$, osmotic pressure.
$\dfrac{p_1^\circ - p_1}{p_1^\circ} = x_2$;  $\Delta T_b = iK_b m$;  $\Delta T_f = iK_f m$;  $\pi = iCRT$.
$K_b$ and $K_f$ depend only on the solvent; units K kg mol$^{-1}$. Water: $K_b$ = 0.52, $K_f$ = 1.86 K kg mol$^{-1}$.
Osmotic pressure is the best method for proteins and polymers: measured at room temperature, uses molarity, and is large even for very dilute solutions.
0.9% (m/V) NaCl is isotonic with blood cells; above it cells shrink (hypertonic), below it they swell (hypotonic).
Reverse osmosis: apply more than the osmotic pressure on the solution side; used to desalinate sea water with cellulose acetate membranes.
$i$ = normal molar mass / abnormal molar mass = observed / calculated colligative property. $i > 1$ dissociation, $i < 1$ association.
mistakes: Using grams of solvent instead of kilograms in molality (divide by 1000).
Using the mass of the solution instead of the mass of the solvent for molality.
Forgetting the van't Hoff factor when the solute is an electrolyte (NaCl: 2, CaCl$_2$ and Na$_2$SO$_4$: 3, Al$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$: 5).
Taking $\Delta T_f$ as the freezing point. The freezing point is $T_f^\circ - \Delta T_f$ (273.15 K - $\Delta T_f$ for water).
Writing 'osmotic pressure is proportional to molality' - it is molarity. $\Delta T_b$ and $\Delta T_f$ use molality.
Saying an ideal solution obeys Henry's law - say it obeys Raoult's law over the entire range of concentration.
Mixing up which deviation gives which azeotrope: positive gives minimum boiling, negative gives maximum boiling.
Comparing equal-percentage solutions by $i$ alone. 1% KCl vs 1% CaCl$_2$: compare $i$ / molar mass (2/74.5 vs 3/111).

Dropping units in the final answer. Several schemes for this unit say so explicitly for a specific question - e.g. 2019 Set 56/3/1 (osmotic pressure), 2023 compartment 56/C/1 and 2024 compartment 56/S/1 (molar mass): deduct half a mark for no or incorrect unit. Not every scheme states it, but always write the unit.
mnemonics: **P**ositive deviation - **P**ushes vapour pressure up, solution boils **lower** (minimum boiling). Negative deviation does the opposite.
Isotonic **'iso = same'**: same osmotic pressure. **Hyper** = more solute (cell shrivels), **hypo** = less solute (cell swells, like a hippo).
**B**oiling uses **K$_b$**, **F**reezing uses **K$_f$**; both use **m**olality. **O**smotic pressure uses **M**olarity - the only one with volume.
examTips: Write the formula first, then substitute with units, then the answer with units. Mark splits differ by question (look at the past-paper solutions on this page for the official split of each); the 2026-27 SQP marking scheme for Q28 gives half marks for its intermediate steps.
For deviation questions write three things: type of deviation, the A-B vs A-A/B-B interaction reason, and the consequence asked (volume change, temperature change, azeotrope type).
In 'which has the lowest freezing point' questions, compare $i 	imes$ concentration. For equal molarities, the solute giving the most ions wins.
For association in benzene, state the equilibrium $2A ightleftharpoons A_2$ and show $i = 1 - \alpha/2$ before solving.
When an assertion-reason pair is about colligative properties, check whether the reason really is the cause (lowering of vapour pressure causes $\Delta T_b$ and $\Delta T_f$).
No calculator: keep fractions until the end and cancel. Most board numbers (31.84/32, 0.512, 1.86 x 0.5) are designed to cancel.
lastMinute: I can define: solution, molarity, molality, mole fraction, ppm, Henry's law, Raoult's law (both forms), ideal solution, azeotrope, colligative property, osmosis, osmotic pressure, isotonic, reverse osmosis, abnormal molar mass, van't Hoff factor.
I can give one example each: ideal pair, positive deviation pair, negative deviation pair, minimum and maximum boiling azeotrope, solid solution with a gas solute (H$_2$ in Pd).
I can draw: vapour pressure vs mole fraction for an ideal solution and for both deviations; vapour pressure vs temperature showing $\Delta T_b$ and $\Delta T_f$.
I can do: molar mass from each colligative property; $i$ and degree of dissociation / association; freezing point of an electrolyte solution.
I know: $K_f$(water) = 1.86, $K_b$(water) = 0.52 K kg mol$^{-1}$; 0.9% NaCl is normal saline; HNO$_3$ azeotrope 68%, 393.5 K; ethanol azeotrope about 95% by volume.
